chapter: Sidney Bechet and the Paris festival
title: The Pumpkin label bootleg of Bechet in Boston
summary: He learns of a bootleg LP from 1951 and talks about bootlegs and unpaid musicians.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: We'll talk about that air check, that was one that was released on the Pumpkin label. I suppose it's a bootleg of some sort even though it does have liner notes and most bootlegs don't have liner notes, you certainly didn't know anything about it being released.

Yes, I called the Union, trying to see if we could get some money out of this down there in Florida, but couldn't do anything about it. It happened so long ago and unless we had a contract with him or had some kind of an agreement, they couldn't do anything, couldn't hurt him any. So like the record business now, it's all bootleg, they call it, you know. I read the other day about Sam Goody and Korvette's, that some of these albums, they are bootleg from tapes and they put them out and they make that money. So when I saw this album, the album is called, 'Sidney Bechet, His Way,' right?
That's right. And it was recorded -- Boston 1951.
1951, I remember that year because Red Richards was there along with Arthur Trappier and

--four men-- myself and we were alternating the bandstand with Stan Getz at the Buckminster Hotel in Boston and I forgot all about that until the fella that recorded me a while back, a couple of years ago, asked me if I knew anything about this record. "You're on this record with Sidney Bechet and the company by the name of Pumpkin label from Miami," and he gave me the darn thing and I listened to it and I liked it but I didn't realize that I played that nice in those years, 1951, wasn't it?
That's right. It's October 15th, 16th and 19th of 1951.

And I intend to tape this and some day maybe I will -- since everybody else is taping to make albums, I think I'll tape some of this and make my own album. What can they do to me? What can they do to those guys? I couldn't do anything with these guys for the Pocket labels, you know.

Yeah. There's also that bootleg that I showed you on Styecon, on the Styecon label, I don't know where it comes from but it is the music recorded at the Stuyvesant Casino with Henry Red Allen, Eddie Price and Buster Bailey. That was probably
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

Right. I remember that time. No, I wouldn't say it was bootleg, it was really -- maybe it was, I'm not sure. I can't say for sure. But talking to other musicians, now, here's an example -- I was talking to Pee Wee Irwin the other day over the telephone, he said, You're right, Chief, that would make quite a bit. I have heard some albums that I have made years ago and I didn't know I was on it with Benny Goodman and I never got paid for it, they're bootleg.

I shouldn't have said he made the album because he didn't make the album. It was taken off an air check like My record was with Sidney Bechet / and put into an album and was sold all over. And they made the money and Pee Wee Irwin never got paid for it. And I don't think Goodman got paid for it.
No doubt he didn't. There are so many of these bootleg -- You got along very well with Bechet and the other --
